title: Design a Learning-to-Rank Search System
prompt: Design the ranking system behind a large-scale search product. Given a user query, it must retrieve candidate documents and rank them so the most relevant appear first, using an ML ranking model with query, document, and user/context features. Assume high query volume, tight latency, and continuous online evaluation.
blurb: Multi-stage retrieval + learning-to-rank: candidate generation, ranking features, training from click logs, and online eval without feedback loops.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (retrieve candidates, rank, personalize, diversify, freshness) from non-functional (p99 latency budget, relevance quality, availability, index freshness).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about corpus size, query volume, latency budget, personalization scope, freshness needs, how relevance is judged (human labels vs clicks).

rubric.label: Back-of-envelope estimations
rubric.description: Derives QPS, index size, per-stage candidate counts and latency, feature fetch QPS, ranking-model inference cost per candidate set.

rubric.label: Multi-stage retrieval architecture
rubric.description: Candidate generation (inverted index / ANN / multiple retrievers) → lightweight L1 ranker → heavy L2 ranker; narrowing candidate count per stage to fit latency.

rubric.label: Ranking features & LTR model
rubric.description: Query, document, query-document match, and user/context features; pairwise/listwise LTR objective (e.g. LambdaMART / neural ranker); feature freshness.

rubric.label: Training-serving parity
rubric.description: Same feature computation offline and online, logging served features + positions, point-in-time correctness, avoiding leakage from future signals.

rubric.label: Training from click logs & bias
rubric.description: Turning clicks into labels, position bias correction (IPS/randomization), selection bias, presentation bias, using human relevance judgments for calibration.

rubric.label: Evaluation & online eval
rubric.description: Offline ranking metrics (NDCG/MAP/MRR), interleaving and A/B tests online, guardrail metrics, detecting relevance/feature drift and feedback loops.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Query understanding → candidate generation → L1 → L2 ranking → blending/diversity → results; async indexing + click-log pipeline feeding training.

rubric.label: Scaling & reliability
rubric.description: Sharded/replicated index, ANN scaling, model-serving fan-out, timeout/partial-results fallback, index update pipeline.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Latency per stage, relevance metrics dashboards, feature freshness/nulls, model version tracking, click-through and abandonment monitoring.

rubric.label: Abuse, fairness & integrity
rubric.description: Spam/SEO manipulation, query privacy, fairness/diversity, preventing ranking-signal gaming and feedback-loop entrenchment.

functional_requirements: Retrieve candidate documents for a query (recall stage)
Rank candidates by predicted relevance (precision stage)
Incorporate personalization and context (user, locale, device, time)
Ensure freshness — newly indexed docs are rankable quickly
Diversify/blend results and apply business rules
Continuously evaluate and improve ranking online
nonfunctional_requirements: End-to-end search latency p99 within budget (e.g. <200ms)
High relevance quality (NDCG) and low abandonment
High availability with graceful partial results
Fresh index (new/updated docs rankable within minutes)
Reproducible ranking: logged features + model version per query
clarifying_questions: Is personalization in scope, and at what granularity?
How fresh must the index be?
How is relevance defined — human judgments, clicks, conversions?
Text-only search or multi-entity (products, media, people)?
qualifying_questions: Single global index or per-locale/vertical indexes?
Do we need strict result diversity or business-rule overrides?

estimations.traffic: ~50K QPS peak; head queries cacheable, long tail must be computed
estimations.index: Billions of documents; sharded inverted index + ANN embeddings; TB-scale
estimations.candidate_funnel: Retrieval ~10K candidates → L1 lightweight ranker → ~500 → L2 heavy ranker → ~50 shown; latency scales with candidate count × model cost
estimations.feature_fetch: L2 scores hundreds of candidates × dozens of features → high feature-store read QPS; precompute doc features offline
estimations.inference: L2 neural ranker ~1-5ms per batch of candidates on GPU/CPU; keep L1 ultra-cheap

core_components: Candidate generation: inverted index + ANN vector retrieval
Feature store (doc features offline + user/context online)
data_model: documents(doc_id PK, fields, embedding, static_features, updated_at)
impressions(query_id, doc_id, position, features_logged, model_version, ts)
api_design: POST /internal/index/upsert { doc } → updates inverted + ANN index
reference.high_level_design: A query first passes through query understanding (normalization, spell/rewrite, intent, query embedding). Candidate generation runs multiple retrievers in parallel — a lexical inverted-index retriever and an ANN embedding retriever — producing a large recall set. A cheap L1 ranker prunes it to a few hundred candidates. The L2 heavy LTR model scores those using query, document, query-doc match, and user/context features fetched from a feature store (doc features precomputed offline; user/context features online). A blending layer applies diversity and business rules to produce the final page. Every impression logs the served features, positions, and model version; clicks/dwell stream into a log pipeline. Offline, clicks are debiased into training labels (position-bias correction), models are retrained and evaluated with NDCG on human-judged and click-derived sets, then rolled out via interleaving and A/B experiments with guardrail metrics.

deep_dives.probe: Design the retrieval stage. How do you combine lexical (inverted index) and semantic (ANN) retrieval, and how many candidates do you pass forward to fit the L2 latency budget?
Your training labels come from clicks, but users click top results regardless of relevance. How do you correct for position/presentation bias — IPS weighting, randomization, an examination model?
How do you ensure the features the L2 model sees at serving time match training exactly? Talk through logging served features and point-in-time joins to avoid leakage.
Offline NDCG improved but that doesn't prove it's better live. How do you evaluate online — interleaving vs A/B — and what guardrail metrics protect against regressions?
The ranker decides what users see, and their clicks train the next ranker. How do you prevent a self-reinforcing feedback loop that entrenches current rankings?
A document is updated or newly published. How quickly is it retrievable and correctly ranked, and how do you avoid serving stale document features?

Document attributes (price, availability, popularity, embeddings) change in a source system. How do those updates propagate into the retrieval index and the feature store so ranking isn't computed on stale doc state?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions feature store or features or embedding
followup_bank.question: When a document's source attributes change (price, stock, popularity, its embedding), how do the index and feature store stay in sync — CDC/change-stream driving re-index + feature recompute, or scheduled batch? What's the freshness bound?

You cache results or features for head queries — what's the eviction/TTL policy, and when a document changes how do you invalidate stale-after-change cache entries so you don't serve outdated rankings?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions click or log or label
followup_bank.question: How do you turn clicks into unbiased training labels — position-bias correction, randomization, or human relevance judgments for calibration?
How do you roll out a new ranking model — interleaving, A/B, guardrail metrics, and rollback on what signal?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions ANN or vector or embedding retrieval
followup_bank.question: How do you scale and update the ANN index, and how do you combine its results with lexical retrieval?
Why can offline NDCG improve while the live experience regresses, and how do you guard against that?

scaling: Shard inverted + ANN index by doc; scatter-gather across shards
Replicate shards for QPS and availability; partial results on shard timeout
Cache results/features for head queries with freshness-aware TTL
Batch L2 scoring; keep L1 ultra-cheap to control fan-out cost
bottlenecks: L2 scoring cost scales with candidate count
Feature fetch fan-out for hundreds of candidates
ANN index build/update cost and memory
tradeoffs: Heavier L2 model (better NDCG) vs inference budget
Clicks (abundant, biased) vs human judgments (clean, scarce) for labels
alternative_solutions: Single-stage BM25/lexical ranking (cheap, no ML) as a baseline/fallback
Cascade with more stages (L0/L1/L2/L3) for very large corpora
Bandit-based exploration to combat feedback loops
observability: Online relevance: CTR, dwell, abandonment, NDCG on judged sets
Feature freshness/null rates; embedding index age
security: Anti-spam / anti-SEO manipulation of ranking signals
Query privacy and PII handling in logs
Fairness and diversity constraints; avoid harmful amplification
reference.tradeoffs_note: The core tension is latency budget vs candidate count vs model complexity across stages.
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer builds a multi-stage funnel — parallel lexical + ANN candidate generation, a cheap L1 pruner, and a heavy L2 LTR model — sizing candidate counts per stage to fit a strict latency budget. It uses query, document, query-doc match, and user/context features, precomputing doc features offline and fetching user/context features online, and trains a pairwise/listwise ranker. It treats click logs as biased signal: correcting position/presentation bias (IPS/randomization), calibrating with human judgments, and guarding against the self-reinforcing feedback loop where the ranker trains on its own exposure. It insists on training-serving parity via logged served features and point-in-time joins, and it evaluates offline with NDCG but proves wins online through interleaving/A-B with guardrail metrics. It keeps the index and feature store fresh via a change-driven reindex/recompute pipeline and monitors relevance, feature freshness, and drift as first-class concerns.
reference.extra: reference_answer above is the canonical strong response

interviewer_notes: Anchor the conversation on the latency budget and force the candidate to justify candidate counts at each stage — this is the crux of ranking-system design. If they jump straight to a fancy model without a retrieval/candidate-generation story, pull them back. Two senior separators: (1) training from biased click logs — make them explain position-bias correction and the feedback-loop risk, not just 'clicks are labels'; and (2) online evaluation — offline NDCG gains must be proven with interleaving/A-B and guardrails, and they should know why offline can improve while live regresses. When they place a feature store or index, hit the CDC/freshness probe: how do source document changes (price, popularity, embeddings) reach the index and feature store. When they add a result/feature cache, probe eviction and stale-after-change invalidation. Also push on training-serving skew via logged served features. Reserve time for drift and safe model rollout. Weak candidates design a single-model ranker; strong ones design a multi-stage retrieval+ranking system with a rigorous, bias-aware training and online-eval loop.
